name: Dupaningan Agta
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Robinson, Laura C. 2008. Dupaningan Agta: Grammar, vocabulary, and texts. PhD dissertation, University of Hawai'i at Manoa. ScholarSpace hdl:10125/20681.
catalog_quote: Stress is phonemic in Dupaningan Agta, but it will not be represented in this work unless it is being specifically discussed. ... Below are minimal and near-minimal stress pairs. ... Any of the five vowels may be stressed. ... When a stressed vowel falls on an open penultimate syllable, it is also long. Stress can fall on open or closed syllables, in any position within the word. ... In suffixed forms, the stress is assigned one syllable later than in the un-suffixed forms. ... But this is not always the case, and the exact conditions of stress assignment under affixation remain unclear.

audit.reasoning: The classification (lexical/phonemic stress, any position, open or closed syllables, minimal pairs; stressed open penults lengthened; affixal stress shift not fully predictable) rests on the sole modern reference grammar of the language (Robinson 2008 PhD, Glottolog 'grammar', 363 pp), and the deciding quotation is verbatim in the text we hold layer at sec. 2.2.2.5, printed pp. 71-72 (locator says 70-72; trivial one-page slip). I downloaded the open-access published edition (Pacific Linguistics 635, 2011) from ANU; its sec. 2.2.2.5 pp. 45-46 repeats the statement word for word with IPA-marked examples, and secs. 3.6/ch. 4 add further stress minimal pairs (anak, agom, payad), all consistent with lexical. Glottolog lists no other grammar or phonology; the author's own survey says prior work is a 1985 stratificational article and unpublished SIL manuscripts; Crossref/Semantic Scholar show no prosody or i

tone.quote: 1.3 Suprasegmental Phonemes. To date, only one suprasegmental phoneme has been established, i.e. stress. There are three degrees of stress: primary, secondary and weak stress. A poly-syllabic word has one primary stress and, if more that three syllables long, has a secondary stress-also. Syllables with neither primary nor secondary stress carry weak stress, as do monosyllabic words mentioned above. Suffixation causes stress to shift. The postulation of stress as a suprasegmental phoneme is based on the contrast evident in several minimal pairs, e.g. ... The majority of the examples above, showing contrastive stress, involve the use of loan words from Ilocano.
tone.summary: No tone: stress is stated to be the only suprasegmental phoneme (contrastive word stress with minimal pairs, three degrees, one primary stress per word, stress shift under suffixation); no tonal or pitch accent contrast posited.
